Some houses are built for arrival. Garran Hill was built for return.
The Page Provenance
Before Garran Hill was an estate,
it was an intention.

Conceived for Walter Hines Page, North Carolina son, man of letters, publisher, reformer, and ambassador, this Pinehurst estate carries the grace of an earlier century into the present day.

Editor of The Atlantic Monthly. Co-founder of Doubleday, Page and Company. Appointed by Woodrow Wilson as Ambassador to the Court of St James's in 1913, and kept there through the years the world came apart.

From London, his imagination kept returning to the Sandhills.

In 1913 he bought a thousand acres of Moore County pine and named it Garran Hill. A gentleman's farm. A peach orchard. A house worthy of return. Six weeks later Wilson sent him to London. He sailed, and the farm stayed behind.

The farm. The farm. The farm.

He wrote home about it constantly. The peaches, the gardens, the pecans. He sent his son Ralph to build it, and asked only to hear of it at every turn.

Build the farm, therefore, and let me hear at every stage of that happy game.

Walter Hines Page, to his son Ralph · March 1918

The Life and Letters of Walter H. Page · Doubleday, Page & Co. · 1923

1915 – 1916

The house rose, built by the Pinehurst Company under J. R. McQueen, the same men then building Pinehurst. Rare handmade brick, laid in Flemish bond above a water table, drawn to Georgian proportion.

Page resigned the embassy and sailed home, gravely ill, in the autumn of 1918.

Well, Frank. I did get here after all, didn't I?

His last recorded words · Aberdeen station · December 1918

He reached Pinehurst that December. Ralph made the farm his home, and the house Page drew from London outlived the longing that built it. He remains the only American diplomat of the First World War honored with a tablet at Westminster Abbey.

The same gate has stood open for more than a century.

The Restoration
By 1998 the house had stood empty.
It was taken down to the studs, and brought back.

It was drawn as it stood, then drawn whole again. Three years to the studs and back. The 1916 fabric kept.

The 1916 fabric kept: seven mantels, the oak, the fanlight, the brass key plates that still turn.

A House of Detail
Nothing asks to be noticed.
Everything rewards attention.

A house tells you what it is in the first three steps. Here, you see straight through to the far windows before the door has closed behind you.

I · First Floor
The Entrance Hall

The mahogany rail leaves the newel in a single unbroken turn and does not let go until the landing. It has been climbed every day since 1916.

The hall opens to the drawing room
II · First Floor
The Drawing Room

Forty feet, and the afternoon crosses all of it. A Federal mantel, a ceiling worked in panels and coffers, bookcases arched into the wall. Two rooms could sit here and never crowd one another.

French doors give onto the brick terrace
III · First Floor
The Library

Shelving to the ceiling on three walls. A house built for a man of letters keeps its promise in this one room.

Through the hall to the sitting room
IV · First Floor
The Sitting Room

Delft tile set around the fire, blue on white. In the corner a spiral stair winds up to the study, the way this house likes to send you somewhere.

The stair climbs to the den above
V · First Floor
The Dining Room

The 1916 frontispiece is still here, and the arched shell cabinets that flank it. The east windows take the morning low and direct.

On to the kitchen
VI · First Floor
The Kitchen

Heart pine underfoot, the one floor that is not the original oak. Black granite, a range under its hood, a butler's pantry with a farm sink. A working room that never forgot the old house around it.

Through to the breakfast room and the grounds
VII · Private Wing
The Primary Suite

A private wing across the full depth of the home. A fireplace in the panels, restored oak, two dressing rooms.

French doors open to the grounds
VIII · Second Floor
The Upstairs Bedrooms

Three more bedrooms above, each with its own fireplace and bath. The Rose, the Yellow, the Red.

Four bedrooms in all
The Grounds
From above,
the estate explains itself.

4.15 acres, Moore County. Garran Hill sits within its own circle, the surviving house core of a much larger Page era farm. Inside the gates: the circular drive, the lawn, the brick walled pool, the tennis courts under the longleaf pines.

IX · The Grounds
The Walled Pool

A saltwater pool set within a brick walled garden. The wall came first.

X · The Grounds
The Courts

Two regulation tennis courts, lit for evening play, under the longleaf pines. The courts await resurfacing, the bones are right.

XI · The Grounds
The Grounds

Mature longleaf pines, Grandiflora magnolias, a camellia garden. And The Wee Cottage in the rear yard.
